introFa: کتاب «Artificial Intelligence: A Guide for Thinking Humans» نوشته Melanie Mitchell یکی از منابع ارزشمند و معتبر برای یادگیری زبان انگلیسی در سطح B2 است. این اثر با ساختاری منسجم و غنی، شما را در تسلط بر واژگان و درک مطلب یاری می‌کند.
readingTipsFa: پیش از مطالعه هر بخش از کتاب «Artificial Intelligence: A Guide for Thinking Humans»، نگاهی سریع به تیترها و ساختار آن بیندازید.
واژگان و اصطلاحات جدید را در زمینه و بافت جمله یادداشت کنید تا در حافظه بلندمدت تثبیت شوند.
پس از پایان هر فصل، نکات کلیدی و آموخته‌های خود را مرور کرده و به زبان خود خلاصه کنید.

content: ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE 233 Book Reviews R.S. Michalski, J.G. Carbonell and T.M. Mitchell, Machine Learning: An Artificial Intelligence Approach (Tioga, Palo Alto, CA); 572 pages, $39.50. Reviewed by: Kurt VanLehn Xerox Palo Alto Research Center, 3333 Coyote Hill Road, Palo Alto, CA 94304, U.S.A. Free Lunches: Knowledge Engineers Welcome This long-awaited volume contains fifteen papers that were presented in July, 1980 at a workshop in Pittsburgh. The workshop was widely perceived as an exciting one which unveiled the first fruits of a renaissance of AI research in learning. This renaissance was seeded, according to some accounts, by Lenat's AM program. AM stunned the AI world by discovering significant conjectures in number theory given only a limited knowledge of set theory and some relatively general heuristics about construction of mathematical conjectures. AM's learning seemed magical, and it still does. No one seems to fully understand just why AM worked so well. (This volume contains one of Lenat's papers on the subject. There have been other papers since.) AM inspired AI researchers to construct learners that worked just as well as AM but were well understood and easily applied to other task domains. Thus, according to certain accounts, was the machine learning movement reborn. Regardless of the origins of the renaissance, there's no denying that machine learning became a popular research area in the late 1970s, and it has been gathering adherents ever since. The papers in this volume are interesting partly for their explicit discussion of the aspirations of the machine learning move- ment. Those discussions will be the focus of this review, but only because it is more fun to talk about why machines should learn than to go over the technical details of how to get machines to learn. The latter question is the main focus of the book and is more important, albeit drier. The radicals in the machine learning movement make the following argument. AI has failed to live up to its initial, naive promise of providing general-purpose problem solvers that exhibit a useful degree of intelligence. Nowadays, it seems that intelligence can be provided, but only by specializing a problem solver for the given task domain. Weak, general-purpose problem- solving methods are just that: weak. There's no free lunch. The problem -solving Artificial Intelligence 25 (1985) 233-239 0004-3702/85/$3.30 © 1985, Elsevier Science Publishers B.V. (North-HoUand)

234 BOOK REVIEWS expertise that one gets out of a program is roughly equal to the special-purpose knowledge that one codes into it. The knowledge engineering movement has adopted a brute-force response to this failure: Since there is no such thing as a universal, intelligent problem solver, the next best thing is to develop tech- nology that makes it easier to code knowledge into special-purpose problem solvers. The radicals in the machine learning movement take a different approach: Although no one can build a problem solver that delivers more intelligence than is coded into it, one might be able to build a learning program that starts dumb and becomes expert by slowly augmenting its initial, built-in knowledge with knowledge acquired from experience, or perhaps from advice given by its users. Lenat's work supported this expectation. He notes that AM acquired mathematical knowledge that was not built into it, and in particular, that some of its acquired knowledge was new to him so he couldn't have built it into AM's initial knowledge base, even indirectly. It seems that AM, and machine learning in general, offers the free lunch that AI had promised but failed to deliver. Needless to say, the radical position on the utility of machine learning is quite controversial. Not every author in this book holds this position, if any do. There is a strong conservative wing in the machine learning movement. The conservatives have demonstrated that there are two areas where machine learning has proven utility. Machine learning is clearly useful as a source of ideas about human learning. Anderson's ACT model of learning (Chapter 7) is a case in point. Other chapters mention, in passing, how their learning programs provide new ways to view human learning. However, the psy- chological utility of machine learning is a minor theme in this book. The second area of demonstrated utility concerns data analysis. There are many ap- plications that involve picking out patterns or clusters in vast quantities of data. Data exploration and analysis is important not only in scientific endeavors, but in commercial applications such as economic forecasting, public health, quality assurance, and many others. Currently available tools (e.g., factor analysis, analysis of variance, multidimensional scaling) have certain disadvantages, which are discussed by Michalski and Stepp in Chapter 11. Machine learning offers analytic techniques without these disadvantages. Five chapters document successful applications of prototype data analysis/exploration tools: Cluster/2 (Michalski and Stepp) finds a taxonomy of concepts, where concepts are represented as property value lists. Star (Michalski) is like Cluster/2, but it employs predicate calculus as its representation of concepts. ID3 (Quinlan) induces an efficient discrimination tree. Bacon (Langley, Bradshaw and Simon) induces polynomials. LMS (Sleeman) induces a best-fitting set of production rules selected from a given stock of rules.

BOOK REVIEWS 235 These works demonstrate the utility of machine learning in the areas of data analysis. Indeed, Cluster/2 and ID3 have survived such thorough testing that they seem close to commercial application. Although the conservatives are enthusiastic about the contributions of machine learning to psychology and data analysis, they are pessimistic about its contributions to knowledge engineering. Simon argues in Chapter 2 that there is no free lunch for knowledge engineers; programming will always be more effective than machine learning for endowing AI systems with the knowledge that they need to perform intelligently. The opposing position is defended by several authors in the form of five machine learners: Lex (Mitchell, Utgoff and Banerji) is a forward-search (antecendent-driven) problem solver that induces better heuristics (conditions) for choosing state- change operators. It has a clean, easily understood architecture. The authors provide an excellent discussion of its weaknesses. Eurisko (Lenat) is similar to Lex in that it is a forward-search problem solver that improves its search by tuning up the heuristics that select the search operator to apply next. The difference is that Lex assumes that a goal state is given, while Eurisko does hill-climbing. Eurisko has been applied to a half- dozen task domains. However, it is still unclear how and why it works. Part of its power seems to lie in its initial knowledge base, which often consists of hundreds of rules, rather than in its extremely simple architecture. Foo (Mostow) is an automatic programming system that is specialized to "write" and "debug" only heuristic search programs. It first instantiates a schema for a means-end problem solver, then it uses optimization trans- formations to improve the solver's effectiveness. Foo is not a complete system. Its user provides the control structure by selecting which instantiation or transformation Foo will apply next. Aries (Carbonell) is a problem solver that maintains and augments a set of linear programs (i.e., pure operator sequences; no branches or loops). Al- though Aries can solve problems directly, using means-end analysis, it prefers to adapt a stored operator sequence to solve the current problem. The adaptation can be a multi-step transformation. Search is required to find it. To guide the search in the transform space, Aries again uses means-ends analysis. Aries was not fully implemented when this chapter was written. Carbonell's more recent papers report that further implementation uncovered fundamental flaws in the design presented in this chapter. Klaus (Hass and Hendrix) is a natural language front end whose lexicon can be extended by the user using only natural language. Although some impressive initial steps have been taken, it is clear from these works that if there is a free lunch for knowledge engineers, it hasn't been found yet. Acquiring knowledge without programming seems feasible when the knowledge is narrowly constrained (e.g., Klaus' lexicon extension task),

236 BOOK REVIEWS or when the learner's initial knowledge base is large and domain-specific (Eurisko?), or when someone just as knowledgeable as a programmer guides the learner (Foo). General-purpose learners, such as Lex and Aries, seem weak. Simon's skepticism is warranted, at least for now. For people who read AI articles as speculative philosophy, two chapters provide fascinating food for thought. Hayes-Roth applies Lakatos' ideas about mathematical proofs and refutations to automatic programming. This is a great idea that should be pushed much further than Hayes-Roth does in his brief chapter. Lenat speculates that Eurisko-like learning might explain several genetic puzzles, such as: why is evolution so rapid, what is the function of the DNA that does not code proteins (it expresses heuristics for mutations, speculates Lenat), and why does the percentage of non-coding DNA increase phylogenetically? For people who teach computer science, this book will be a good set of readings for a graduate course on machine learning. The overview articles (Chapters 1, 3 and 4) and the bibliography may be particularly useful to students. However, the book would have to be supplemented by material on grammar induction, adaptive control and multidimensional scaling (at least), since it ignores non-AI forms of machine learning. R.S. In his review of Machine Learning Kurt VanLehn provides the perspective of an active researcher in machine learning. In contrast, this review is from the perspective of an outsider using the book to get an introduction. The hardback publication of the workshop proceedings created high expectations for me, and I set aside an unfettered weekend to read them and to savor the ideas and insights. There were many questions: What's happening in machine learning? Why has there been a sudden renewal of interest? Has there been a flurry of results? Is the field converging on specific approaches? Are there design principles for creating learning systems? As VanLehn said in his review, there are "no free lunches" yet, and the prognosis is murky.
